intro: ENT covers the ear, nose, throat and neck problems that fill Australian general practice and emergency departments: ear infections, sore throat, nosebleeds, hearing loss, vertigo, neck lumps and airway emergencies. The AMC tests antibiotic stewardship in common infections, the higher-risk approach needed for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander ear disease and rheumatic fever, and the red flags (sudden hearing loss, airway compromise, head and neck cancer) that must never be missed.

lessons.title: Ear pain and otitis
objectives: Diagnose acute otitis media, otitis media with effusion and otitis externa from history and otoscopy
Decide when a child with AOM needs amoxicillin and when watchful waiting is safe
Manage chronic suppurative otitis media with ear toilet and topical ciprofloxacin
Recognise the ear emergencies: mastoiditis, necrotising otitis externa and cholesteatoma
Explain why ear disease in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children is a public health priority

sections.heading: Why ears matter in Australia
sections.body:
Ear pain is one of the commonest reasons children see a GP in Australia, and almost every child has at least one episode of acute otitis media (AOM) before school age. Most AOM is self-limiting. The AMC therefore tests two opposite skills: **not** giving antibiotics to the well child who will get better, and **not missing** the child who needs them.

The second theme is **First Nations ear health**. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, especially in remote communities, have some of the highest rates of chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) in the world. Infection starts in the first weeks of life, recurs constantly and often goes unnoticed because it is painless. The result is conductive hearing loss during the years when speech and language develop, with downstream effects on schooling, behaviour and later life. This is why Australian guidance treats ear disease in these children more actively, and why every state runs universal newborn hearing screening plus targeted ear checks.

The five ear conditions to know cold:

| Condition | Key picture |
|---|---|
| AOM | Acute pain, fever, bulging red drum |
| Otitis media with effusion (glue ear) | No pain, dull retracted drum, hearing loss |
| Otitis externa | Painful tragus, swollen canal with debris |
| CSOM | Painless persistent discharge through a perforation |
| Cholesteatoma | Foul discharge, attic retraction or pocket with keratin |

sections.heading: How middle and outer ear infections develop
sections.body:
**AOM** follows a viral upper respiratory infection. Mucosal swelling blocks the Eustachian tube, middle ear secretions cannot drain, and nasopharyngeal bacteria (*Streptococcus pneumoniae*, non-typeable *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Moraxella catarrhalis*) multiply in the trapped fluid. Children are prone because their Eustachian tube is shorter, more horizontal and floppier. Daycare, passive smoking, bottle feeding lying down and crowding increase the risk.

**Otitis media with effusion (OME)** is fluid without acute inflammation. It often follows AOM and resolves over weeks to months as the tube starts working again.

**CSOM** develops when the drum perforates and the middle ear mucosa stays chronically infected, typically with *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* and *Staphylococcus aureus*. In remote communities, early colonisation of the nasopharynx with multiple pathogens, crowded housing and limited access to clean water drive a cycle of repeated perforation.

**Cholesteatoma** is skin in the wrong place: a retraction pocket (usually in the attic, the pars flaccida) traps keratinising squamous epithelium, which accumulates, becomes infected and erodes bone. Left untreated it can destroy the ossicles, expose the facial nerve and cause intracranial infection.

**Otitis externa** is infection of the canal skin, usually *Pseudomonas* or *S. aureus*, sometimes fungal. Moisture (swimming, humidity), trauma (cotton buds, hearing aids) and eczema break the protective skin and wax barrier. In older people with diabetes or immunosuppression it can spread to the skull base as **necrotising (malignant) otitis externa**.

sections.heading: History and otoscopy
sections.body:
**AOM:** a young child with a cold who becomes irritable, febrile, pulls at the ear and sleeps poorly. Otoscopy shows a **red, bulging** tympanic membrane with loss of the light reflex. Bulging is the most specific sign; redness alone happens with crying and fever. If the drum perforates, pain suddenly eases and pus appears in the canal.

**OME:** no pain or fever. Parents or teachers notice the child does not listen, has the TV loud, or has speech delay. The drum is dull, retracted or amber with a fluid level or bubbles, and moves poorly on pneumatic otoscopy. Tympanometry gives a **flat (type B)** trace.

**Otitis externa:** pain, itch and discharge. The hallmark is **pain on moving the tragus or pinna**, which does not happen in AOM. The canal is swollen, red and full of debris; the drum may be hard to see.

**CSOM:** painless discharge persisting for weeks (commonly defined as more than 2 weeks) through a visible perforation, with conductive hearing loss. A child who "just has runny ears" in a remote community has CSOM until proven otherwise.

**Cholesteatoma:** chronic, foul-smelling discharge that does not settle with drops, hearing loss, and an attic perforation or retraction pocket with white keratin debris. Vertigo or facial weakness means erosion into the inner ear or facial canal.

**Mastoiditis:** a child with AOM who becomes more unwell, with **post-auricular swelling, tenderness and redness** and the pinna pushed forward and down.

**Necrotising otitis externa:** an elderly person with diabetes, severe night-time ear pain out of proportion to the findings, granulation tissue on the canal floor, and sometimes lower cranial nerve palsies (facial nerve first).

sections.heading: What to test
sections.body:
Most ear infections are clinical diagnoses. Tests are for the chronic, atypical or complicated case.

- **Pneumatic otoscopy and tympanometry**: confirm middle ear fluid (type B flat trace) in OME, or a perforation (high canal volume).
- **Audiology**: formal hearing assessment for persistent OME (around 3 months), CSOM and any child with speech delay or school concerns.
- **Ear swab** for microscopy and culture: CSOM or otitis externa not responding to treatment, and necrotising otitis externa.
- **Blood glucose / HbA1c**: in anyone with severe or recurrent otitis externa, to look for diabetes.
- **CT temporal bones** (with contrast if abscess suspected): suspected mastoiditis, cholesteatoma planning, necrotising otitis externa. MRI helps for intracranial complications.
- **ESR/CRP**: useful to monitor necrotising otitis externa over weeks of treatment.

sections.heading: Australian management
sections.body:
**AOM (eTG):**
- All children: **analgesia** (paracetamol or ibuprofen) is the priority. Explain that most improve within 24-72 hours without antibiotics, and arrange review or a clear plan to return.
- **Give amoxicillin** when the benefit is greater: infants under 6 months; children under 2 with **bilateral** AOM; AOM with **perforation or discharge**; a systemically unwell child; high-risk groups, particularly **Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children**; and failure to improve after 48-72 hours of watchful waiting. A 5-day course is standard for uncomplicated AOM; check eTG for current doses and for longer courses in high-risk groups.
- Penicillin allergy (non-severe) or treatment failure: follow eTG alternatives rather than reaching reflexively for broad-spectrum agents.
- Recurrent AOM or persistent OME with hearing loss: refer to ENT for consideration of **grommets (tympanostomy tubes)**.

**OME:** watchful waiting for about 3 months, since most resolve. Arrange a hearing test if it persists. Refer for grommets if there is persistent bilateral effusion with hearing loss, speech or learning problems, or structural drum changes. Antibiotics, antihistamines and decongestants do not help.

**Otitis externa:**
- **Aural toilet** first: dry mopping or suction microscopy so drops reach the skin.
- **Topical combination antibiotic-steroid drops** (for example framycetin-gramicidin-dexamethasone, or ciprofloxacin-hydrocortisone) for about 7 days. If the canal is too swollen for drops to enter, insert an **ear wick**.
- Keep the ear dry; avoid cotton buds. Oral antibiotics only if cellulitis spreads beyond the canal.
- **Necrotising otitis externa**: admit, IV antipseudomonal antibiotics, ENT and glucose control.

**CSOM:**
- **Ear toilet** (dry mopping with tissue spears, or suction) at least daily, then **topical ciprofloxacin drops** twice daily, continued until the ear has been dry for several days.
- Ciprofloxacin is preferred because aminoglycoside-containing drops carry a risk of ototoxicity when the drum is perforated.
- Refer to ENT and audiology; persistent perforations may need tympanoplasty once the ear is dry.

**Mastoiditis and cholesteatoma:** admit mastoiditis for IV antibiotics and imaging, with surgery for abscess. Cholesteatoma always needs surgery (mastoidectomy); drops only settle the discharge.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- **Tragal tenderness** separates otitis externa from AOM. A red bulging drum with no canal swelling is AOM.
- A well 3-year-old with unilateral AOM for one day: the answer is **analgesia and review**, not antibiotics.
- The same child but **Aboriginal**, under 6 months, bilateral under 2, or with discharge: **amoxicillin**.
- "Runny ears for months, painless, perforation" in a remote community child: **CSOM → ear toilet + topical ciprofloxacin**, plus hearing assessment. Oral antibiotics alone are the trap.
- Foul discharge that won't settle plus attic pocket: **cholesteatoma**, refer for surgery.
- Elderly diabetic with severe pain and granulation tissue: **necrotising otitis externa**, admit.
- A child with speech delay and a dull, retracted drum: think **OME and hearing**, not behaviour.

keyPoints: Most AOM resolves in 1-3 days; analgesia is always first line.
Amoxicillin for AOM if under 6 months, bilateral under 2, discharge, unwell, First Nations child, or no improvement at 48-72 h.
Pain on moving the tragus means otitis externa: aural toilet plus steroid-antibiotic drops, wick if swollen.
CSOM is painless persistent discharge through a perforation: ear toilet plus topical ciprofloxacin.
OME causes hearing loss without pain; watch for 3 months, then audiology and grommets if persistent.
Foul chronic discharge with an attic pocket is cholesteatoma and needs surgery.
Post-auricular swelling with a pushed-forward pinna is mastoiditis: admit.
redFlags: Post-auricular swelling or pinna displaced forward (mastoiditis)
Severe ear pain with granulation tissue in an elderly diabetic (necrotising otitis externa)
Facial weakness, vertigo or headache with chronic ear discharge (cholesteatoma or intracranial spread)
Neck stiffness, drowsiness or high fever with otitis media (meningitis, intracranial abscess)
Speech delay or school problems in a child with recurrent ear disease

contrast.india: An oral antibiotic is usually prescribed at the first visit.
contrast.australia: Analgesia and watchful waiting with review at 48-72 hours; antibiotics reserved for defined high-risk groups.

contrast.india: Often oral antibiotics plus referral for surgery.
contrast.australia: Daily ear toilet with topical ciprofloxacin in primary care, hearing assessment, and community ear-health programs for First Nations children.

flashcards.front: Most specific otoscopic sign of AOM?
flashcards.back: A **bulging** tympanic membrane (redness alone is non-specific).

flashcards.front: First-line antibiotic for AOM when one is indicated?
flashcards.back: **Amoxicillin**, typically a 5-day course for uncomplicated AOM (eTG).

flashcards.front: Topical treatment of CSOM?
flashcards.back: Ear toilet, then **ciprofloxacin drops** twice daily until dry. Avoid aminoglycoside drops with a perforation.

flashcards.front: Tympanogram in otitis media with effusion?
flashcards.back: **Flat, type B** trace (fluid in the middle ear).

flashcards.front: Sign that separates otitis externa from AOM?
flashcards.back: Pain on moving the **tragus or pinna**.

flashcards.front: Organism in necrotising otitis externa?
flashcards.back: *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, usually in elderly people with diabetes.

quiz.stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to a GP in suburban Melbourne with 24 hours of right ear pain following a cold. He is miserable but playing in the waiting room. Temperature is 38.2°C. The right tympanic membrane is red and bulging; the left is normal. There is no discharge. He has no allergies and is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

What is the most appropriate management?
options: Analgesia with review if not improving in 48-72 hours
quiz.explanation:
This is **unilateral AOM in a well child over 2** from a low-risk group. Most such children improve within 1-3 days without antibiotics, and antibiotics give only a small reduction in pain at the cost of diarrhoea, rash and resistance. Australian guidance (eTG) is **analgesia (paracetamol or ibuprofen) and watchful waiting**, with a clear plan to return or be reviewed if he is not improving after 48-72 hours, or sooner if worse.

Antibiotics would be indicated if he were under 6 months, under 2 with bilateral disease, had discharge or perforation, was systemically unwell, or was a First Nations child.
whyWrong: Amoxicillin is reserved for higher-risk children; this well boy over 2 with unilateral AOM does not meet the criteria.
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is not first line even when antibiotics are indicated.
Topical ciprofloxacin is for CSOM or discharging ears, not an intact drum.
Myringotomy is not indicated for a first uncomplicated episode.
quiz.ausPearl: eTG frames AOM antibiotic decisions around risk groups; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children are treated more readily because of CSOM and hearing loss risk.

quiz.stem:
A 7-year-old Aboriginal girl from a remote community in the Northern Territory is seen by the visiting doctor. Her mother says her left ear has been 'running' on and off for months, but she has no pain or fever. Otoscopy after cleaning shows a central perforation of the left tympanic membrane with mucopurulent discharge. The right ear is normal.

What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Watchful waiting and review in 3 months
Daily ear toilet and topical ciprofloxacin drops
quiz.explanation:
Painless, persistent discharge through a perforation is **chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM)**. The organisms are usually *Pseudomonas* and *S. aureus*, which oral amoxicillin does not reliably cover and which sit in the discharge where systemic antibiotics penetrate poorly.

Treatment is **ear toilet** (dry mopping with tissue spears or suction) so drops reach the mucosa, followed by **topical ciprofloxacin drops** until the ear is dry. Ciprofloxacin is chosen because aminoglycoside drops risk ototoxicity through a perforation. She also needs a **hearing assessment** and ongoing follow-up through the community ear-health program, since CSOM in First Nations children causes conductive hearing loss that affects speech and education.
whyWrong: Oral amoxicillin does not reliably cover Pseudomonas and is not first-line for CSOM.
Aminoglycoside-containing drops carry an ototoxicity risk with a perforated drum.
CSOM needs active treatment; waiting perpetuates hearing loss.
Mastoidectomy is for cholesteatoma or complications, not uncomplicated CSOM.
quiz.ausPearl: Australia has among the highest CSOM rates in the world in remote Aboriginal communities; ear health is a national public health priority.

quiz.stem:
A 74-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presents to a regional emergency department with 3 weeks of severe left ear pain that keeps him awake at night, despite a course of antibiotic ear drops from his GP. There is purulent discharge and granulation tissue on the floor of the external canal. He has a mild left lower motor neurone facial weakness. Temperature is 37.4°C.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the ear canal
quiz.explanation:
The combination of an **elderly person with diabetes**, **severe night pain out of proportion** to the findings, **granulation tissue on the canal floor** and **facial nerve palsy** is classic for **necrotising (malignant) otitis externa**. It is an osteomyelitis of the skull base, usually caused by *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, spreading from the external canal through the fissures of Santorini. The facial nerve is the first cranial nerve affected as it exits the stylomastoid foramen.

Management is admission, cultures, CT or MRI to define the extent, prolonged IV antipseudomonal antibiotics per eTG, ENT review and tight glucose control. Canal SCC is an important differential, so biopsy of persistent granulation tissue is often performed.
whyWrong: Cholesteatoma causes chronic foul discharge from the middle ear via an attic defect, usually without severe night pain.
Mastoiditis causes post-auricular swelling and usually follows AOM.
Ramsay Hunt syndrome causes vesicles in the canal or pinna with facial palsy, not granulation tissue.
Canal SCC is a differential worth biopsying, but the diabetic context and pain pattern point to infection.

lessons.title: Sore throat, quinsy and deep neck infections
objectives: Decide who needs antibiotics for sore throat using acute rheumatic fever risk, not the look of the tonsils
Prescribe the eTG regimen for streptococcal pharyngitis in a high-risk patient
Recognise and manage peritonsillar abscess, epiglottitis and Ludwig angina
Distinguish glandular fever from bacterial tonsillitis and avoid the amoxicillin rash
Know the indications for tonsillectomy and how to handle post-tonsillectomy bleeding

sections.heading: The Australian approach to sore throat
sections.body:
Sore throat is extremely common and mostly **viral**. Even when group A *Streptococcus* (GAS, *S. pyogenes*) is the cause, antibiotics shorten symptoms by only about a day in most people. Australia has high antibiotic prescribing rates for sore throat, and national stewardship campaigns target this.

The real reason to treat GAS pharyngitis in Australia is **prevention of acute rheumatic fever (ARF)** and rheumatic heart disease (RHD). Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people living in remote and regional northern Australia have some of the highest rates of ARF and RHD in the world, and Māori and Pacific Islander people are also at high risk. So the key question the AMC wants you to ask is not "does this throat look bacterial?" but **"is this person at high risk of rheumatic fever?"**

High risk (per eTG and the Australian ARF/RHD guideline) includes:
- Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people living in rural or remote areas, or in high-ARF settings
- Māori and Pacific Islander people
- People with a personal history of ARF or RHD
- Others living in crowded, socioeconomically disadvantaged settings where ARF is common

In low-risk people, antibiotics are generally reserved for severe illness, suppurative complications (quinsy) or scarlet fever.

sections.heading: From throat infection to complications
sections.body:
**Viral pharyngitis** (rhinovirus, adenovirus, influenza, SARS-CoV-2) usually comes with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis.

**GAS pharyngitis** is more likely with fever, tender anterior cervical nodes, tonsillar exudate and **absence of cough** (the basis of the Centor and FeverPAIN scores, which you should know about but which do not override risk-based decisions in Australia).

**ARF** follows untreated GAS infection by 2-4 weeks. Antibodies against streptococcal antigens cross-react with cardiac, joint, brain and skin tissue (**molecular mimicry**). Repeated attacks scar the valves, especially the mitral, producing RHD. In northern Australia, GAS **skin sores (impetigo)** are probably as important as sore throats as a trigger.

**Suppurative complications** arise when infection spreads beyond the tonsil:
- **Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)**: pus between the tonsil capsule and the superior constrictor, usually in adolescents and young adults.
- **Parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal abscess**: deeper spread; retropharyngeal is mainly in young children.
- **Ludwig angina**: rapidly spreading cellulitis of the floor of the mouth (submandibular and sublingual spaces), usually from a lower molar dental infection, which pushes the tongue up and back and obstructs the airway.

**Epiglottitis** (supraglottitis) is bacterial cellulitis of the epiglottis. Since Hib vaccination it is now seen more in **adults** than children, from a mix of organisms.

**Infectious mononucleosis** (EBV) causes exudative tonsillitis with generalised lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, mainly in teenagers and young adults.

sections.heading: Recognising each picture
sections.body:
| Condition | Discriminating features |
|---|---|
| Viral pharyngitis | Cough, coryza, hoarseness, conjunctivitis |
| GAS tonsillitis | Fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes, no cough |
| Glandular fever | Teen or young adult, marked fatigue, posterior cervical nodes, palatal petechiae, splenomegaly |
| Quinsy | Worsening unilateral throat pain, **trismus**, **uvula deviated away**, muffled "hot potato" voice, drooling, referred ear pain |
| Epiglottitis | Rapid onset, severe odynophagia out of proportion to a near-normal oropharynx, drooling, muffled voice, stridor, sitting forward (tripod) |
| Retropharyngeal abscess | Young child, fever, neck stiffness or reluctance to extend the neck, drooling |
| Ludwig angina | Recent dental pain, brawny swelling under the jaw, raised tongue, can't swallow saliva |

**Scarlet fever**: GAS with a sandpaper rash, flushed cheeks with circumoral pallor and strawberry tongue.

A key AMC clue in epiglottitis: **the throat looks relatively normal** yet the patient is in agony and cannot swallow saliva. The inflammation is below what you can see.

sections.heading: Tests that change management
sections.body:
- **Throat swab** for culture (or rapid antigen test where available): mainly in **high-risk** people, so that a positive result can be notified to the ARF/RHD register where relevant and the diagnosis confirmed. Do not delay antibiotics in high-risk patients while waiting for the result.
- **ASOT and anti-DNase B**: to support a diagnosis of ARF, not to diagnose pharyngitis.
- **FBE and EBV serology / monospot**: suspected glandular fever (atypical lymphocytes; monospot can be negative early and in young children). LFTs are often mildly deranged.
- **Quinsy**: a clinical diagnosis. CT neck with contrast if deep neck space infection is suspected or the diagnosis is uncertain.
- **Epiglottitis**: **do not** examine the throat with a tongue depressor or send the patient alone to radiology. Visualisation is by flexible nasendoscopy in a controlled setting with airway expertise present. A lateral neck X-ray may show the "thumb sign", but it is not needed if the diagnosis is clear.
- **Ludwig angina**: CT once the airway is secured or judged safe; orthopantomogram (OPG) for the dental source.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.body:
**Sore throat, low risk:** analgesia (paracetamol, ibuprofen), fluids, salt-water gargles or lozenges, and a safety-net about quinsy and airway symptoms. Explain that antibiotics add little.

**Sore throat, high risk of ARF (eTG):** **phenoxymethylpenicillin for 10 days**. The 10-day course matters: shorter courses do not reliably eradicate GAS from the pharynx, and eradication is what prevents ARF. Where adherence to 10 days is unlikely, a **single IM dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin** is an equally effective alternative. For penicillin allergy follow eTG alternatives. Check eTG for weight-based doses.

**Glandular fever:** supportive. **Avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin**, which causes a widespread maculopapular rash in most people with EBV (not a true penicillin allergy). Advise **avoiding contact sports** for several weeks because of splenic rupture risk. Steroids only for airway compromise from tonsillar swelling.

**Quinsy:**
- Needle **aspiration or incision and drainage** of the abscess, usually by ENT.
- **IV antibiotics** (eTG: benzylpenicillin-based regimen), analgesia, IV fluids if not drinking. A dose of corticosteroid is often given to reduce swelling.
- Recurrent quinsy is an indication for tonsillectomy.

**Epiglottitis:** keep the patient calm and sitting up, give oxygen, **call senior anaesthetics and ENT**, and secure the airway in theatre if needed. IV antibiotics (eTG recommends ceftriaxone-based therapy) once the airway plan is in place, with corticosteroid often added.

**Ludwig angina:** airway first (awake fibreoptic intubation or surgical airway), IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering oral anaerobes, surgical drainage and dental extraction.

**Tonsillectomy:** consider for recurrent tonsillitis (commonly cited thresholds: 7 or more episodes in 1 year, 5 per year for 2 years, or 3 per year for 3 years), recurrent quinsy, and **obstructive sleep apnoea** in children.

**Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage** is an emergency. **Primary** bleeding occurs within 24 hours (surgical); **secondary** bleeding occurs typically at 5-10 days, associated with infection of the tonsil bed. Any bleeding after tonsillectomy needs ED review, IV access, bloods and group and hold, and ENT.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- A 22-year-old Sydney university student with exudative tonsillitis and no risk factors: usually **no antibiotics**.
- A 12-year-old Aboriginal child in a remote community with a sore throat: **phenoxymethylpenicillin for 10 days** (or IM benzathine benzylpenicillin), regardless of how the throat looks.
- Trismus + uvula deviated away from the swollen side + hot potato voice = **quinsy → drain and IV antibiotics**.
- Adult with severe odynophagia, drooling and a **normal-looking oropharynx** = **epiglottitis**: do not use a tongue depressor; call for airway help.
- Rash after amoxicillin in a teenager with sore throat and splenomegaly = **EBV**, not penicillin allergy.
- Bleeding a week after tonsillectomy = **secondary haemorrhage**, go to hospital.

keyPoints: Most sore throats are viral; the reason to treat GAS in Australia is preventing acute rheumatic fever.
High ARF risk (many First Nations communities, Māori, Pacific Islander, prior ARF/RHD): phenoxymethylpenicillin 10 days or one IM benzathine benzylpenicillin.
Quinsy: trismus, uvula deviation, hot potato voice; drain and give IV antibiotics.
Epiglottitis is now mainly an adult disease; don't examine the throat, secure the airway first.
Amoxicillin in EBV causes a rash; avoid contact sports for several weeks because of the spleen.
Ludwig angina is a dental-origin floor-of-mouth cellulitis that threatens the airway.
Secondary post-tonsillectomy bleeding occurs around days 5-10 and needs hospital review.
redFlags: Drooling or inability to swallow saliva
Stridor, muffled voice or tripod posture
Trismus with unilateral peritonsillar swelling
Floor-of-mouth swelling with a raised tongue after dental infection
Any bleeding after tonsillectomy

contrast.aspect: Who gets antibiotics for sore throat
contrast.india: Decided largely on exudate and fever; amoxicillin or azithromycin is widely used.
contrast.australia: Decided on acute rheumatic fever risk; phenoxymethylpenicillin for 10 days in high-risk people, usually none in low-risk.

contrast.india: Taught as a paediatric Hib disease.
contrast.australia: Hib vaccination has made it mostly an adult disease; AMC stems often feature an adult with a normal-looking throat.

flashcards.back: **Phenoxymethylpenicillin for 10 days**, or a single IM dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin.

flashcards.front: Three signs of peritonsillar abscess?
flashcards.back: **Trismus**, **uvula deviated away** from the abscess, muffled "hot potato" voice.

flashcards.front: Why avoid amoxicillin in suspected glandular fever?
flashcards.back: It causes a **maculopapular rash** in most people with EBV.

flashcards.front: Timing of secondary post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage?
flashcards.back: Typically **5-10 days** after surgery, linked to infection of the tonsil bed.

flashcards.front: Origin of Ludwig angina?
flashcards.back: **Lower molar dental infection** spreading to the submandibular and sublingual spaces.

quiz.stem:
A 13-year-old Aboriginal boy living in a remote community in the Kimberley presents to the community clinic with 2 days of sore throat and fever of 38.4°C. He has tender anterior cervical lymph nodes and mildly enlarged tonsils without exudate. He has no cough. He has no known allergies and no past history of rheumatic fever.

What is the most appropriate management?
options: Analgesia only and review in 3 days
Throat swab and treat only if culture is positive
quiz.explanation:
This boy is at **high risk of acute rheumatic fever**: he is an Aboriginal child living in a remote community in northern Australia, where ARF and RHD rates are among the highest in the world. In high-risk people, eTG recommends treating sore throat presumptively with **phenoxymethylpenicillin for 10 days** (or a single IM dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin if adherence is a concern). A swab can be taken, but treatment should not wait for the result.

The 10-day duration is essential because the goal is **eradication** of GAS from the pharynx to prevent ARF, not symptom relief. How the tonsils look is irrelevant to this decision.
whyWrong: Withholding antibiotics is appropriate in low-risk people, not in a high-risk child.
Amoxicillin is not the eTG first line, and 5 days is too short to reliably eradicate GAS.
Treatment should not be delayed for a swab result in a high-risk patient.
Macrolides are reserved for penicillin allergy and resistance is a concern.
quiz.ausPearl: Confirmed ARF and RHD are notifiable in several jurisdictions, and state RHD registers manage secondary prophylaxis with 4-weekly benzathine benzylpenicillin.

quiz.stem:
A 24-year-old woman presents to an emergency department in Brisbane with 4 days of worsening left-sided sore throat. She can barely open her mouth, is drooling, and her voice sounds muffled. Temperature is 38.6°C, heart rate 108/min, SpO2 98% on room air. There is no stridor. Examination shows swelling above and lateral to the left tonsil with the uvula pushed to the right.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin and review in 48 hours
Needle aspiration or incision and drainage with IV antibiotics
quiz.explanation:
Unilateral throat pain, **trismus**, **drooling**, a **muffled hot potato voice** and **uvular deviation away** from a swelling superolateral to the tonsil are the classic features of a **peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)**. She is maintaining her airway (no stridor, normal saturations).

Treatment is to **drain the pus** (needle aspiration or incision and drainage, usually by ENT under local anaesthetic) plus **IV antibiotics** per eTG, analgesia and fluids. Corticosteroids are commonly added. Oral antibiotics alone are inadequate once an abscess has formed. Tonsillectomy is considered later for recurrent quinsy, rather than as the first step.
whyWrong: Oral antibiotics alone will not treat an established abscess.
Glandular fever does not cause unilateral peritonsillar swelling with uvular deviation.
Quinsy is a clinical diagnosis; imaging is only needed if deeper spread is suspected.
Tonsillectomy is not the first-line treatment of an acute quinsy.

quiz.stem:
A 48-year-old man presents to an emergency department in Adelaide with 8 hours of rapidly worsening throat pain. He is sitting upright leaning forward, drooling into a cup and speaking in a muffled voice. Temperature is 38.9°C, heart rate 118/min, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 95% on room air. There is soft inspiratory stridor. A glimpse of the oropharynx while he speaks shows only mild erythema.

What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Examine the pharynx with a tongue depressor to look for a quinsy
Send for a CT scan of the neck
Give oral phenoxymethylpenicillin and discharge with safety-netting
Keep him sitting up and call senior anaesthetic and ENT staff to secure the airway
Lie him flat and insert an oropharyngeal airway
quiz.explanation:
Severe odynophagia, **drooling**, muffled voice, **tripod posture** and **stridor** with an oropharynx that looks almost normal is **acute epiglottitis (supraglottitis)**. Since Hib vaccination this is now more common in adults. The swelling is at the supraglottis, below what you can see through the mouth.

The immediate priority is the **airway**: keep him calm and sitting up, give oxygen, and call **senior anaesthetics and ENT** so that the airway can be assessed by nasendoscopy and secured in a controlled setting, with surgical airway backup. IV antibiotics and corticosteroids follow once the airway plan is in place. Instrumenting the throat, lying him flat or sending him to CT can precipitate complete obstruction.
whyWrong: A tongue depressor can provoke laryngospasm and complete obstruction.
An unstable airway must never go to the scanner without being secured.
This is a life-threatening airway emergency, not a simple sore throat.
Lying flat worsens obstruction, and an oropharyngeal airway will not bypass supraglottic swelling.

lessons.title: Epistaxis, sinusitis and nasal problems
objectives: Give correct first aid for epistaxis and escalate stepwise to cautery, packing and ENT
Tell anterior from posterior epistaxis and manage anticoagulated patients sensibly
Diagnose acute rhinosinusitis and recognise orbital complications
Manage a nasal fracture, including the septal haematoma that must not be missed
Identify sinister unilateral nasal symptoms and nasal foreign bodies in children

sections.heading: Why the nose is examinable
sections.body:
Nosebleeds are one of the commonest ENT presentations to Australian emergency departments and general practice. Most are anterior, minor and stop with correct first aid, but older patients on anticoagulants or antiplatelets can bleed heavily from the posterior nose and become haemodynamically unstable.

The AMC also tests the nose through **acute rhinosinusitis** (mostly viral; antibiotic stewardship again), **allergic rhinitis** (very common in Australia, which has high rates of asthma and hay fever, and thunderstorm asthma events in Victoria), **nasal trauma** (the septal haematoma trap), **children with foreign bodies**, and **unilateral symptoms in adults** that may signal sinonasal cancer.

sections.heading: Where the blood comes from
sections.body:
About 90% of nosebleeds are **anterior**, from **Little's area** on the anterior septum, where the **Kiesselbach plexus** (branches of the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries) lies just under thin mucosa. Dry air, nose picking, colds, allergic rhinitis and nasal steroid sprays used against the septum all damage it. This is typical in **children and young adults**.

**Posterior** bleeds come from branches of the **sphenopalatine artery** and are more common in **older people** with hypertension, atherosclerosis, and anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy. Blood runs down the back of the throat, both nostrils may bleed, and anterior pressure does not stop it.

Other causes to keep in mind:
- **Coagulopathy**: warfarin, DOACs, antiplatelets, liver disease, haemophilia, von Willebrand disease, thrombocytopenia (leukaemia).
- **Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT)**: recurrent epistaxis with telangiectasia on lips and tongue, and a family history.
- **Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma**: recurrent severe unilateral epistaxis with nasal obstruction in an **adolescent male**.
- **Sinonasal malignancy**: unilateral bloody discharge and obstruction in an older adult (woodworkers and leather workers are at increased risk of adenocarcinoma).

**Acute rhinosinusitis** is usually a viral URTI involving the sinuses. Bacterial superinfection (*S. pneumoniae*, *H. influenzae*, *M. catarrhalis*) is suggested by symptoms lasting **more than 10 days**, **double sickening** (improvement then worsening), or severe pain and high fever. Ethmoid infection can spread through the thin lamina papyracea to the orbit.

sections.heading: Assessment
sections.body:
**Epistaxis:** assess ABC first. Pale, sweaty, tachycardic or hypotensive patients need resuscitation before anything else. Then ask: which side, how long, how much, swallowing blood, previous episodes, anticoagulants and antiplatelets, alcohol and liver disease, bruising elsewhere, and family history. Examine with a headlight and nasal speculum after clearing clots. Check blood pressure, but remember that high BP in epistaxis is often due to anxiety and is not treated acutely.

**Rhinosinusitis:** nasal obstruction, purulent discharge, facial pain or pressure worse on bending forward, reduced smell. **Chronic rhinosinusitis** is symptoms for 12 weeks or more, with or without nasal polyps (think aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease if polyps plus asthma).

**Orbital complications (periorbital and orbital cellulitis)** are an emergency:
- **Preseptal** cellulitis: swollen red eyelids but normal eye movements, acuity and pupils.
- **Orbital (postseptal)** cellulitis: **proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, reduced visual acuity or colour vision**, relative afferent pupillary defect.

**Allergic rhinitis:** sneezing, itchy watery eyes and nose, clear rhinorrhoea, seasonal (spring grass pollen) or perennial (house dust mite). Pale boggy turbinates; allergic salute crease in children.

**Nasal fracture:** deformity, swelling and epistaxis after trauma. Always look inside for a **septal haematoma**: a boggy, fluctuant, purple bilateral swelling of the septum that blocks the nose.

**Nasal foreign body:** a young child with **unilateral foul-smelling purulent discharge**, sometimes blood-stained.

sections.heading: Investigations
sections.body:
- **Epistaxis**: none for a simple anterior bleed in a young person. For significant bleeding, recurrent bleeds or older patients: **FBE** (haemoglobin, platelets), **coagulation studies/INR** if on warfarin or liver disease suspected, **group and hold** for heavy bleeding. Nasendoscopy by ENT for recurrent or posterior bleeds.
- **Acute rhinosinusitis**: a clinical diagnosis. No imaging for uncomplicated disease. **CT sinuses and orbits with contrast** if orbital or intracranial complications are suspected.
- **Chronic rhinosinusitis or unilateral symptoms**: nasendoscopy and CT sinuses; biopsy of any mass.
- **Allergic rhinitis**: skin prick testing or specific IgE if the allergen is unclear or immunotherapy is being considered.
- **Nasal fracture**: X-rays are **not** needed for an isolated nasal fracture; the diagnosis and the decision to reduce are clinical. CT if other facial fractures are suspected.
- **Button battery** suspected in the nose: urgent removal; do not wait for imaging if the history is clear.

sections.heading: Stepwise management
sections.body:
**Epistaxis ladder:**
1. **First aid**: sit up, **lean forward**, breathe through the mouth, spit out blood, and **pinch the soft (cartilaginous) part of the nose firmly for 10-15 minutes** without letting go to check. An ice pack on the bridge or sucking ice may help. Leaning back makes the patient swallow blood and vomit.
2. If still bleeding: clear clots, apply a **topical vasoconstrictor with local anaesthetic** (for example co-phenylephrine/lignocaine spray, or cotton pledgets soaked in it) and re-pinch.
3. **Cautery** of a visible anterior bleeding point with a **silver nitrate** stick, working from the periphery in. **Cauterise one side of the septum only** at a time: cauterising both sides risks septal perforation.
4. If cautery fails or no point is seen: **anterior nasal packing** (an inflatable balloon pack or expanding sponge). Packed patients usually need review and ENT follow-up; packs stay in for about 24-48 hours.
5. **Posterior bleeding**: posterior pack or balloon (a Foley catheter can be used in an emergency), admit, and involve ENT. Refractory bleeding: endoscopic **sphenopalatine artery ligation** or interventional radiology **embolisation**.

**Anticoagulated patients:** most bleeds settle with local measures. Check INR, and do not routinely stop or reverse anticoagulation for a controlled bleed; discuss with the prescriber. Reverse only for life-threatening haemorrhage (for example vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate for warfarin; idarucizumab for dabigatran).

**After cautery:** avoid nose blowing, heavy lifting, hot drinks and exertion for about a week. An antiseptic nasal cream (chlorhexidine-neomycin) is often used; note it contains **peanut (arachis) oil**, so check for peanut allergy.

**Acute rhinosinusitis:** analgesia, saline irrigation, and intranasal corticosteroids. Antibiotics only if bacterial features are present (over 10 days, double sickening, or severe); eTG recommends **amoxicillin** as first line. Orbital cellulitis: admit, IV antibiotics, urgent ophthalmology and ENT, CT.

**Allergic rhinitis:** allergen avoidance, saline, **intranasal corticosteroid** as the most effective regular treatment, non-sedating oral or intranasal antihistamines, and a combination intranasal steroid-antihistamine spray for moderate to severe disease. Refer for allergen immunotherapy if symptoms persist. Remember the link with asthma.

**Nasal fracture:** treat any septal haematoma **the same day** by incision and drainage, then packing and antibiotics; otherwise the cartilage necroses (**saddle nose**) or forms an abscess. For the fracture itself, reassess once swelling settles at about **5-7 days**; closed reduction, if needed, is best done within about 2 weeks.

**Nasal foreign body:** try the **"parent's kiss"** (positive pressure through the mouth with the clear nostril occluded) or remove with a hook under direct vision. **Button batteries** are an emergency because they cause rapid liquefactive necrosis.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- First aid answer: **sit up, lean forward, pinch the soft part for 10-15 minutes**. Head back and pinching the bony bridge are the classic wrong answers.
- Cautery is **silver nitrate, one side of the septum only**.
- A 76-year-old on apixaban with bleeding from both nostrils and blood down the throat despite anterior packing: **posterior epistaxis → posterior pack, admit, ENT**.
- Teenage boy with recurrent heavy unilateral bleeds and obstruction: **juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma**; do not biopsy in the clinic.
- After a punch to the nose: **look for septal haematoma**; no X-ray needed.
- Toddler with unilateral smelly discharge: **foreign body**.
- Swollen eyelids with proptosis or reduced acuity: **orbital cellulitis**, not preseptal.

keyPoints: Epistaxis first aid: sit up, lean forward, pinch the soft part of the nose for 10-15 minutes.
Most bleeds are anterior from Little's area; posterior bleeds occur in older, hypertensive or anticoagulated patients.
Silver nitrate cautery to one side of the septum only, then packing, then ENT.
Anticoagulation is not routinely reversed for a controlled nosebleed.
Bacterial sinusitis: over 10 days, double sickening or severe; amoxicillin first line.
Proptosis, painful eye movements or reduced vision with sinusitis means orbital cellulitis.
A septal haematoma after nasal trauma must be drained the same day to prevent saddle nose.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability or ongoing bleeding down the throat
Recurrent unilateral epistaxis with obstruction in an adolescent male
Unilateral bloody discharge or obstruction in an older adult
Proptosis, ophthalmoplegia or reduced acuity with sinusitis
Septal haematoma after nasal trauma
Button battery in the nose

contrast.aspect: Epistaxis first aid taught to the public
contrast.india: Head tilted back and cold compresses are still commonly advised.
contrast.australia: Lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for 10-15 minutes, as taught in first aid courses and ED handouts.

contrast.india: Nasal bone X-rays are frequently ordered.
contrast.australia: Isolated nasal fractures are a clinical diagnosis; review at 5-7 days, and X-ray is not required.

flashcards.back: Sit up, **lean forward**, pinch the **soft part** of the nose for **10-15 minutes** without releasing.

flashcards.front: Site of most anterior nosebleeds?
flashcards.back: **Little's area** (Kiesselbach plexus) on the anterior septum.

flashcards.back: Cartilage necrosis causing **saddle nose** deformity, or septal abscess.

flashcards.back: At about **5-7 days**, once swelling settles; reduce within about 2 weeks.
