flashcards.back: **Peanut (arachis) oil**: check for peanut allergy.

quiz.stem:
A 9-year-old girl is brought to a GP clinic in Perth with a nosebleed from the left nostril that started 5 minutes ago while playing. Her mother has been holding a tissue under her nose with her head tilted back. She is pink and well perfused, heart rate 96/min.

What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Silver nitrate cautery to the left side of the septum
Sit her up, lean her forward and pinch the soft part of her nose for 10-15 minutes
Apply an ice pack to the back of her neck with her head tilted back
Arrange a full blood examination and coagulation studies
quiz.explanation:
Most childhood nosebleeds are **anterior**, from **Little's area**, and stop with correct first aid. The patient should **sit up and lean forward** (so blood drains out rather than being swallowed and causing vomiting or airway soiling), breathe through the mouth, and have the **soft, cartilaginous part of the nose pinched firmly for 10-15 minutes** without releasing to check.

Head tilted back is the classic error. Cautery and packing are the next steps only if first aid fails. Blood tests are not needed in a well child with a first minor bleed, but recurrent heavy bleeds or bruising elsewhere would prompt an FBE and coagulation screen.
whyWrong: Cautery is used only if first aid fails and a bleeding point is seen.
Packing is a later step for bleeding that continues despite first aid and cautery.
Tilting the head back makes her swallow blood; neck ice has no proven effect.
Blood tests are not needed for a single minor anterior bleed in a well child.

quiz.stem:
A 78-year-old man on apixaban for atrial fibrillation presents to an emergency department in Hobart with 2 hours of heavy nosebleed. Blood is coming from both nostrils and he is spitting blood from the back of his throat. Anterior pressure for 15 minutes and a well-placed anterior balloon pack in the right nostril have not stopped it. Heart rate is 106/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg. Haemoglobin is 112 g/L.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Silver nitrate cautery to both sides of the septum
Posterior nasal packing, admission and urgent ENT review
Discharge with the pack in place and GP review in 48 hours
Give idarucizumab to reverse the anticoagulant
Lower his blood pressure with IV labetalol
quiz.explanation:
Bleeding from **both nostrils** and down the **back of the throat** that continues despite correct anterior pressure and an anterior pack indicates a **posterior epistaxis**, usually from branches of the sphenopalatine artery. It is typical of older, anticoagulated patients.

The next step is a **posterior pack or balloon** (a Foley catheter in an emergency), **admission**, IV access, bloods including group and hold, and **urgent ENT** for endoscopic control, sphenopalatine artery ligation or embolisation if packing fails. Discuss anticoagulation with the treating team, but specific reversal is reserved for life-threatening bleeding. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, not apixaban.
whyWrong: Bilateral septal cautery risks perforation, and cautery does not reach a posterior source.
A posterior bleed in an anticoagulated, tachycardic older man needs admission.
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only; reversal is not first line for a bleed controllable with packing.
Elevated BP in epistaxis is usually reactive; his BP is not high and lowering it is not the priority.

quiz.stem:
A 19-year-old man presents to a GP in Darwin the day after being punched in the nose at a party. His nose is swollen and slightly deviated to the left and he has bilateral nasal obstruction. Speculum examination shows a smooth, purple, fluctuant swelling on both sides of the nasal septum. His vision and eye movements are normal.

What is the most appropriate management?
options: Nasal bone X-ray and review in 1 week
Oral antibiotics and nasal decongestant spray
Same-day referral for incision and drainage
Closed reduction of the fracture in 5-7 days
quiz.explanation:
The bilateral, fluctuant, purple septal swelling is a **septal haematoma**. Blood collects between the cartilage and the perichondrium, which is the cartilage's blood supply. Without prompt drainage the cartilage **necroses within days**, causing a **saddle nose** deformity, or the haematoma becomes infected to form a septal abscess.

He needs **same-day** ENT or ED referral for **incision and drainage**, followed by packing and antibiotics. The fracture itself is managed separately: isolated nasal fractures are clinical diagnoses without X-ray, reassessed at about 5-7 days once the swelling settles, with closed reduction within about 2 weeks if the deformity is significant.
whyWrong: X-rays do not change management of isolated nasal fractures and a septal haematoma cannot wait a week.
Antibiotics alone will not decompress the haematoma or prevent cartilage necrosis.
Fracture reduction can wait, but the haematoma cannot.
Reassurance misses a problem that will destroy the septal cartilage.

lessons.title: Hearing loss, vertigo and facial palsy
objectives: Separate conductive from sensorineural hearing loss with Rinne and Weber tests
Treat sudden sensorineural hearing loss as an emergency and refer for steroids
Distinguish BPPV, vestibular neuritis, Ménière disease and posterior circulation stroke
Investigate unilateral sensorineural hearing loss or tinnitus for vestibular schwannoma
Manage Bell palsy and recognise Ramsay Hunt syndrome and upper motor neurone weakness

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.body:
About one in six Australians has some hearing loss, most commonly age-related, and hearing loss is increasingly recognised as a modifiable risk factor for dementia. Dizziness is one of the commonest reasons older people present to GPs and emergency departments. The AMC tests three reasoning skills here:

1. **Localise hearing loss** at the bedside (conductive vs sensorineural) and know which causes are urgent.
2. **Recognise sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL)** as an emergency, because the window for steroid treatment is short.
3. **Tell peripheral from central vertigo**, because a cerebellar or brainstem stroke can look like "labyrinthitis".

Facial nerve palsy sits here because the nerve runs through the temporal bone and several ear conditions affect it.

sections.heading: Mechanisms
sections.body:
**Conductive hearing loss (CHL)**: sound fails to reach the cochlea. Causes: **wax**, otitis externa, foreign body, **perforation**, **OME**, AOM, cholesteatoma, and **otosclerosis** (fixation of the stapes footplate; young adults, often a family history, may worsen in pregnancy).

**Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL)**: damage to the cochlea or cochlear nerve.
- **Presbycusis**: bilateral, symmetrical, high-frequency loss with age.
- **Noise-induced**: characteristic dip ("notch") at **4 kHz** on audiometry; occupational noise and recreational exposure.
- **Ototoxic drugs**: **aminoglycosides** (gentamicin), **cisplatin**, high-dose loop diuretics, high-dose aspirin (often reversible tinnitus).
- **Sudden SNHL**: mostly idiopathic (viral or vascular theories). A minority are due to vestibular schwannoma, stroke or autoimmune disease.
- **Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)**: benign tumour of the vestibular nerve Schwann cells causing **unilateral** progressive SNHL and tinnitus; bilateral tumours suggest neurofibromatosis type 2.
- **Congenital**: congenital CMV, genetic causes; detected by universal newborn hearing screening.

**Vertigo** is an illusion of movement, usually rotational, from asymmetry between the two vestibular systems.
- **BPPV**: otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) dislodge into a semicircular canal, usually the **posterior** canal, so that head movement causes fluid to move abnormally.
- **Vestibular neuritis**: presumed viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve; hearing is spared. **Labyrinthitis** involves the labyrinth, so hearing is also lost.
- **Ménière disease**: endolymphatic hydrops producing attacks of vertigo with fluctuating hearing loss.
- **Central vertigo**: posterior circulation stroke or TIA, vestibular migraine, multiple sclerosis, cerebellopontine angle tumours.

**Bell palsy** is an idiopathic lower motor neurone facial palsy, probably due to viral (HSV) inflammation and swelling of the nerve in the narrow facial canal. **Ramsay Hunt syndrome** is varicella zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion.

sections.heading: Bedside assessment
sections.body:
**Tuning fork tests (512 Hz):**

| Finding | Conductive loss (left) | Sensorineural loss (left) |
|---|---|---|
| Rinne, left | **Negative**: bone louder than air | Positive: air louder than bone (both reduced) |
| Weber | Lateralises **to the left** (affected) | Lateralises **to the right** (good ear) |

A useful memory: Weber goes **toward** a conductive loss and **away** from a sensorineural loss.

**SSNHL:** sudden (over less than 72 hours), usually unilateral hearing loss, often noticed on waking or on the phone, with tinnitus, aural fullness and sometimes vertigo. The ear looks **normal** on otoscopy, and Weber lateralises to the good ear. Patients and doctors often wrongly attribute it to wax or "fluid".

**Vertigo patterns:**

| Condition | Duration | Hearing | Key feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| BPPV | Seconds (under 1 minute) | Normal | Triggered by rolling over, looking up; **positive Dix-Hallpike** |
| Vestibular neuritis | Continuous for days | Normal | Recent viral illness; unidirectional horizontal nystagmus; abnormal head impulse test |
| Labyrinthitis | Days | **Lost** | As neuritis plus hearing loss |
| Ménière disease | 20 minutes to 12 hours | **Fluctuating low-frequency SNHL** | Tinnitus and aural fullness; recurrent attacks |
| Posterior circulation stroke | Continuous | Usually normal (can be lost in AICA stroke) | Vascular risk factors, inability to walk, other neurology, abnormal HINTS |

**HINTS examination** (for a patient with acute continuous vertigo and nystagmus): a **normal head impulse test**, **direction-changing nystagmus**, or **skew deviation** on cover testing each suggest a **central** cause. Remember: an abnormal (corrective saccade) head impulse is reassuring because it means the peripheral nerve is the problem. Severe truncal ataxia (cannot sit or walk unaided) is also central.

**Dix-Hallpike:** turning the head 45° to one side and lying the patient back quickly with the head hanging produces, after a short latency, **torsional upbeating nystagmus** that fatigues within a minute, with vertigo, when the undermost ear is affected.

**Facial palsy:** a **lower motor neurone** lesion paralyses the **whole of one side** including the **forehead**. An **upper motor neurone** lesion (stroke) **spares the forehead** because it has bilateral cortical supply. Bell palsy comes on over hours to 2-3 days, sometimes with ear pain, hyperacusis and altered taste. **Ramsay Hunt**: vesicles in the ear canal or on the pinna, severe ear pain, and often SNHL or vertigo.

sections.heading: Investigations
sections.body:
- **Pure tone audiometry**: confirms type and severity of hearing loss; urgent in suspected SSNHL. SSNHL is usually defined as a loss of **at least 30 dB over 3 contiguous frequencies** developing within 72 hours.
- **Tympanometry**: type B (flat) suggests middle ear fluid or perforation.
- **MRI of the internal acoustic meati (with gadolinium)**: for **unilateral or asymmetric SNHL**, **unilateral tinnitus**, and after SSNHL, to exclude vestibular schwannoma.
- **Acute vertigo**: bloods and ECG as needed; **urgent brain imaging (MRI preferred, CT angiography if MRI unavailable)** when HINTS suggests a central cause or there are neurological signs, a new severe headache, or inability to walk. A normal early CT does not exclude posterior fossa stroke.
- **Bell palsy**: clinical diagnosis after excluding other causes on examination (ears, parotid, other cranial nerves, limbs). Check glucose in diabetics. Image if atypical: slowly progressive, recurrent on the same side, other cranial nerve involvement, or no recovery at 3-4 months (think parotid or skull base tumour).

sections.heading: Management
sections.body:
**SSNHL is an emergency.** Refer the same day or next day to ENT for audiometry and **high-dose oral corticosteroid (prednisolone)**, ideally started as soon as possible; benefit falls away if started beyond about 2 weeks. Intratympanic steroids are used as salvage. Arrange MRI.

**Wax:** ceruminolytic drops (for example olive oil or sodium bicarbonate drops) for a few days, then irrigation or microsuction. **Do not syringe** with a known perforation, previous ear surgery, or active otitis externa.

**Chronic hearing loss:** audiology and **hearing aids**. The Australian Government **Hearing Services Program** funds devices for eligible people (pensioners, veterans and others), and **Hearing Australia** provides services for children and young adults under 26 and First Nations people. Cochlear implants for severe to profound SNHL. Otosclerosis: hearing aid or stapedectomy. Protect hearing at work (state work health and safety noise regulations). Review ototoxic drugs; monitor gentamicin levels.

**BPPV:** the **Epley manoeuvre** (canalith repositioning) cures most posterior canal BPPV at the first attempt; it can be repeated and patients can be taught home exercises. Vestibular suppressants are not needed.

**Vestibular neuritis:** short course of antiemetic or vestibular suppressant (for example prochlorperazine) for the first days only, because prolonged use delays central compensation; early mobilisation and vestibular rehabilitation. Some clinicians give early corticosteroids.

**Ménière disease:** acute attacks with vestibular suppressants; long term, low-salt diet, betahistine is commonly used though evidence is mixed, and ENT for refractory disease (intratympanic therapy).

**Posterior circulation stroke:** stroke pathway, urgent imaging and consideration of reperfusion.

**Driving:** vertigo, sudden hearing loss and stroke can affect fitness to drive. Advise the patient according to Austroads **Assessing Fitness to Drive**, and check its current criteria.

**Bell palsy:**
- **Oral prednisolone within 72 hours** of onset improves recovery.
- **Eye protection** is essential: lubricating drops by day, ointment and taping the eye shut at night, sunglasses. Incomplete eye closure risks exposure keratitis.
- Antivirals alone do not help; adding one to steroids may be considered in severe palsy.
- About 70-85% recover fully, most within 3 months. Refer if not improving.

**Ramsay Hunt:** prednisolone **plus an antiviral** (valaciclovir or famciclovir), analgesia, eye care and ENT review. Recovery is worse than Bell palsy.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- "Woke up deaf in one ear, ear looks normal, Weber to the other side": **SSNHL → urgent ENT for steroids**, not wax drops or antibiotics.
- Unilateral tinnitus or asymmetric SNHL: **MRI IAM** for vestibular schwannoma.
- Brief vertigo rolling over in bed: **BPPV → Dix-Hallpike then Epley**.
- Days of vertigo after a cold, normal hearing, abnormal head impulse: **vestibular neuritis**.
- Episodic vertigo lasting hours with fluctuating hearing and fullness: **Ménière**.
- Older vasculopath with continuous vertigo, **normal head impulse** or direction-changing nystagmus, can't walk: **stroke**.
- Forehead spared: **UMN (stroke)**, not Bell palsy. Vesicles in the ear canal: **Ramsay Hunt**, add antiviral.
- Bell palsy question stems nearly always want **steroids within 72 hours plus eye protection**.

keyPoints: Weber goes toward a conductive loss and away from a sensorineural loss; Rinne is negative in conductive loss.
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an emergency: urgent ENT, oral steroids, then MRI.
Unilateral SNHL or tinnitus needs MRI of the internal acoustic meati for vestibular schwannoma.
BPPV: seconds of positional vertigo, positive Dix-Hallpike, treated with the Epley manoeuvre.
In acute continuous vertigo, a normal head impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus or skew suggests stroke.
Ménière: attacks of 20 min to 12 h with fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness.
Bell palsy involves the forehead; give prednisolone within 72 hours and protect the eye.
redFlags: Sudden hearing loss with a normal-looking ear
Unilateral progressive hearing loss or tinnitus
Acute vertigo with inability to walk, new headache, diplopia, dysarthria or limb signs
Normal head impulse test or direction-changing nystagmus in continuous vertigo
Facial weakness sparing the forehead, or with other cranial nerve or limb signs
Facial palsy that progresses slowly or fails to recover by 3-4 months

contrast.india: Often first treated as wax or Eustachian tube dysfunction with decongestants.
contrast.australia: Treated as an emergency: same-day ENT or audiology, prompt oral steroids and MRI.

contrast.india: Mostly self-funded and taken up late.
contrast.australia: Government Hearing Services Program and Hearing Australia fund devices for eligible groups, including children and First Nations people.

flashcards.front: Weber result in left conductive hearing loss?
flashcards.back: Lateralises **to the left** (the affected ear).

flashcards.front: Urgent treatment of sudden sensorineural hearing loss?
flashcards.back: **High-dose oral corticosteroid** via urgent ENT referral, ideally within days.

flashcards.front: Nystagmus on a positive Dix-Hallpike test?
flashcards.back: **Torsional upbeating** nystagmus after a short latency, fatiguing within a minute.

flashcards.front: HINTS finding reassuring for a peripheral cause?
flashcards.back: An **abnormal head impulse test** (corrective saccade) with unidirectional nystagmus and no skew.

flashcards.front: Bell palsy treatment window for prednisolone?
flashcards.back: **Within 72 hours** of onset, plus eye protection.

flashcards.front: Classic audiogram finding in noise-induced hearing loss?
flashcards.back: A notch at **4 kHz**.

quiz.stem:
A 46-year-old accountant presents to her GP in Canberra saying she woke up 2 days ago unable to hear from her right ear, with ringing and a blocked feeling. She has no pain, discharge or recent illness. Otoscopy shows normal ear canals and tympanic membranes. Weber test lateralises to the left and Rinne test is positive bilaterally.

What is the most appropriate management?
options: Olive oil drops and review in 1 week
Pseudoephedrine and a nasal steroid spray
Urgent ENT referral for audiometry and oral corticosteroids
quiz.explanation:
Sudden unilateral hearing loss with **normal otoscopy**, Weber lateralising **away** from the affected ear and a **positive Rinne** (air conduction better than bone) indicates **sudden sensorineural hearing loss** of the right ear. It is an **otological emergency**: the chance of recovery improves when high-dose **oral corticosteroids** are started early, with benefit declining if treatment is delayed beyond about 2 weeks.

She needs urgent (same-day or next-day) ENT review and audiometry to confirm the loss, steroids, and an **MRI of the internal acoustic meati** to exclude vestibular schwannoma. Treating it as wax or Eustachian tube dysfunction is the classic trap that loses the treatment window.
whyWrong: The canals are clear; wax treatment delays time-critical steroid therapy.
Decongestants treat Eustachian tube dysfunction, which causes conductive loss with Weber to the affected side.
There is no infection, and antibiotics have no role in SSNHL.
Waiting 6 weeks loses the window for effective treatment.
quiz.ausPearl: In Australia SSNHL is commonly managed through ED or on-call ENT the same day; many GP guidelines explicitly warn against assuming Eustachian tube dysfunction.

quiz.stem:
A 62-year-old woman presents to her GP in Newcastle with 1 week of brief spinning episodes, each lasting about 20 seconds, when she rolls over in bed or looks up to hang washing. Between episodes she feels well. Hearing is normal and there are no neurological symptoms. On testing, turning her head to the right and lying her back quickly produces vertigo and torsional upbeating nystagmus after a few seconds, which settles within 30 seconds.

What is the most appropriate management?
quiz.explanation:
Brief (**seconds**) episodes of vertigo **triggered by head position** with normal hearing, and a **positive right Dix-Hallpike** (latency, torsional upbeating nystagmus, fatigue within a minute), is **benign paroxysmal positional vertigo** of the right posterior semicircular canal.

The treatment is the **Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre**, which moves the otoconia out of the canal and cures most patients in one or two sessions. Patients can be taught home exercises for recurrences. Vestibular suppressants do not treat the cause and can slow compensation.
whyWrong: Vestibular suppressants do not fix BPPV and prolonged use delays compensation.
Betahistine and salt restriction are used for Ménière disease.
Classic BPPV with a typical Dix-Hallpike and no neurological features does not need imaging.
Steroids are used in SSNHL or vestibular neuritis, not BPPV.

quiz.stem:
A 71-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and a 40 pack-year smoking history presents to an emergency department in Wollongong with 6 hours of continuous vertigo, nausea and vomiting. He cannot walk without falling. Hearing is normal. He has horizontal nystagmus beating to the left on left gaze and to the right on right gaze. The head impulse test is normal in both directions. CT brain is normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
quiz.explanation:
In an **acute vestibular syndrome** (continuous vertigo, nystagmus, nausea), the **HINTS** examination separates peripheral from central causes. He has two central features: **direction-changing nystagmus** and a **normal head impulse test** (in vestibular neuritis the head impulse is abnormal, with a corrective saccade). Add **severe gait ataxia** and multiple vascular risk factors, and this is a **posterior circulation (cerebellar or brainstem) stroke** until proven otherwise.

A normal CT does not exclude it, since CT is insensitive in the posterior fossa. He needs urgent **MRI (with diffusion-weighted imaging)** or CT angiography and the stroke team.
whyWrong: Vestibular neuritis gives an abnormal head impulse and unidirectional nystagmus, and patients can usually walk.
BPPV causes brief positional episodes, not continuous vertigo.
Ménière attacks come with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness.
Labyrinthitis causes hearing loss and a peripheral HINTS pattern.

quiz.stem:
A 35-year-old man presents to a GP in Geelong with a day of drooping of the right side of his face. He noticed a dull ache behind his right ear yesterday and drinks now dribble from the right side of his mouth. He cannot wrinkle his right forehead or fully close his right eye. There are no vesicles in the ear or mouth, and the rest of the neurological examination is normal.

What is the most appropriate management?
quiz.explanation:
Acute unilateral facial weakness **involving the forehead** is a **lower motor neurone** lesion. With post-auricular ache, no vesicles and an otherwise normal neurological examination, this is **Bell palsy**.

**Oral prednisolone within 72 hours** of onset improves the rate of full recovery. **Eye protection** is equally important because he cannot close the eye: lubricating drops by day, ointment and taping at night, and sunglasses, to prevent exposure keratitis. Antivirals alone do not help (they may be added to steroids in severe cases). Refer if weakness progresses or there is no recovery by 3-4 months.
whyWrong: Forehead involvement makes this a lower motor neurone lesion, not a stroke.
Antivirals alone are ineffective in Bell palsy; they are added in Ramsay Hunt.
Steroids within 72 hours improve outcomes and the eye needs protection.
Surgical decompression has no routine role in Bell palsy.

lessons.title: Neck lumps, head and neck cancer and stridor
objectives: Recognise the red flags for head and neck cancer and refer promptly
Work up an adult neck lump with ultrasound and fine needle aspiration rather than open biopsy
Differentiate congenital, inflammatory, salivary and malignant neck lumps by site and history
Assess stridor and manage upper airway emergencies including anaphylaxis and ACE inhibitor angioedema

sections.heading: The picture in Australia
sections.body:
Head and neck cancers are mostly **squamous cell carcinomas (SCC)** of the mouth, pharynx and larynx. In Australia the classic patient is an older man who smokes and drinks, but the fastest-growing group is **HPV-related oropharyngeal SCC** (tonsil and base of tongue) in younger, often non-smoking adults. Australia's high UV exposure also means **lip SCC** (usually the lower lip) and cutaneous SCC metastasising to parotid and neck nodes are common. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is more common in people of southern Chinese and South-East Asian background, and oral cancer is associated with betel quid and chewing tobacco, relevant for migrant communities from South Asia.

The HPV vaccine, given to all adolescents through the National Immunisation Program, is expected to reduce oropharyngeal cancer over time.

Most adult neck lumps are **reactive lymph nodes**, but a **persistent neck lump in an adult is malignant until proven otherwise**, and the way you investigate it matters.

sections.heading: Red flags and how neck lumps present
sections.body:
**Head and neck cancer red flags** (refer promptly, typically to ENT or a head and neck clinic):
- **Persistent hoarseness for more than 3 weeks**, especially in a smoker (laryngeal cancer; the vocal cord needs to be seen)
- **Neck lump** persisting beyond about 3 weeks in an adult
- **Unilateral ear pain with a normal ear** (referred otalgia via the glossopharyngeal or vagus nerve from the tonsil, tongue base, pharynx or larynx)
- **Dysphagia or odynophagia**, persistent sore throat, especially unilateral
- Non-healing mouth ulcer or red/white patch (erythroplakia, leukoplakia) beyond about 3 weeks
- **Unilateral nasal obstruction or bloody discharge**
- **Unilateral middle ear effusion in an adult** (nasopharyngeal carcinoma blocking the Eustachian tube)
- Stridor, weight loss, haemoptysis, cranial nerve palsies

**Neck lumps by site and age:**

| Lump | Clues |
|---|---|
| Reactive lymph node | Recent URTI, tender, small, resolves within weeks |
| **Thyroglossal duct cyst** | Midline, **moves up on tongue protrusion** and swallowing, child or young adult |
| **Branchial cyst** | Anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, young adult, may enlarge with URTI; cholesterol crystals on aspiration. In an adult over about 40, a "branchial cyst" may be a cystic SCC metastasis (often HPV oropharyngeal) |
| Cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation) | Infant, posterior triangle, transilluminates |
| Thyroid nodule | Midline or paramedian, moves on swallowing (not tongue protrusion) |
| **Pleomorphic adenoma** | Slow-growing painless parotid lump, commonest salivary tumour |
| Salivary malignancy | Rapid growth, pain, fixity, **facial nerve palsy** |
| Submandibular stone (sialolithiasis) | Pain and swelling of the submandibular gland **on eating** |
| Lymphoma | Rubbery, painless nodes, B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss) |
| Metastatic SCC | Hard, fixed, upper or mid jugular node in an older smoker or HPV-positive younger adult |
| TB lymphadenitis | Migrant from high-prevalence country, matted nodes, possible sinus |

**Stridor** is a harsh sound from turbulent flow through a narrowed upper airway. **Inspiratory** stridor suggests obstruction at or above the vocal cords; **expiratory** suggests intrathoracic tracheal obstruction; **biphasic** suggests subglottic or fixed tracheal narrowing. In adults the causes to think of are **anaphylaxis**, **angioedema** (especially on an ACE inhibitor), **epiglottitis**, deep neck infection, **foreign body**, laryngeal or tracheal tumour, bilateral vocal cord palsy (for example after thyroid surgery) and inhalational burns.

sections.heading: Working up a neck lump and hoarseness
sections.body:
**Adult neck lump persisting beyond about 3 weeks:**
1. **Full head and neck examination**, including oral cavity, oropharynx, ears, skin of the scalp and face (cutaneous SCC and melanoma metastasise to neck and parotid nodes), thyroid, and other node groups.
2. **Ultrasound of the neck** with **ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration (FNA)** (or core biopsy in selected cases, for example suspected lymphoma).
3. Referral to ENT/head and neck surgery for **flexible nasendoscopy** to look for a primary.
4. **CT or MRI** of the neck, and PET-CT for staging or an unknown primary; HPV (p16) testing on the tissue.

**Do not perform an open excision biopsy of a suspicious neck node as the first step.** If the node is a metastatic SCC, open biopsy can seed tumour and compromise the definitive neck dissection or radiotherapy plan.

**Hoarseness over 3 weeks:** direct visualisation of the larynx (flexible nasendoscopy by ENT). If the cause is a vocal cord palsy, image the course of the recurrent laryngeal nerve (CT from skull base to mediastinum) to look for lung apex, thyroid or mediastinal pathology.

**Salivary lumps:** ultrasound and FNA; avoid open biopsy of a parotid lump (risk to the facial nerve and tumour spillage). Sialolithiasis: ultrasound or CT.

**Stridor:** the diagnosis is clinical and treatment comes first. Once stable, nasendoscopy, CT neck and chest, and bronchoscopy as needed. Tryptase within a few hours helps confirm anaphylaxis retrospectively.

sections.heading: Telling the look-alikes apart
sections.body:
| Presentation | Benign explanation | Sinister explanation | Discriminator |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hoarseness | Viral laryngitis, voice overuse, reflux, vocal nodules | Laryngeal SCC, recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (lung, thyroid cancer) | Duration over 3 weeks, smoking, stridor, weight loss |
| Earache | Otitis externa, AOM, TMJ dysfunction, dental | Referred pain from oropharyngeal or laryngeal cancer | Normal ear examination plus dysphagia or smoker |
| Adult unilateral glue ear | Post-URTI Eustachian tube dysfunction | Nasopharyngeal carcinoma | Persistent, unilateral, adult, Asian background, neck node |
| Lateral cystic neck lump | Branchial cyst | Cystic nodal metastasis from HPV oropharyngeal SCC | Age over 40, persistence, tonsil asymmetry |
| Angioedema | Allergic (histamine) with urticaria | Bradykinin-mediated: ACE inhibitor, hereditary angioedema | No urticaria or itch, on ACE inhibitor, poor response to adrenaline |

sections.heading: Management and referral
sections.body:
**Suspected head and neck cancer:** refer promptly to ENT or a head and neck surgical service; Cancer Council Australia's **Optimal Care Pathway** for head and neck cancers sets out expected timeframes and multidisciplinary team (MDT) care. Treatment is by an MDT (surgeon, radiation and medical oncologist, speech pathologist, dietitian, dentist, psychologist): surgery, radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy depending on site and stage. HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer has a better prognosis. **Smoking cessation** improves treatment outcomes and should be addressed at diagnosis. Pre-radiotherapy **dental assessment** reduces osteoradionecrosis risk. Long-term issues include dysphagia, dry mouth, hypothyroidism after neck radiotherapy, and psychological distress.

**Benign lumps:** thyroglossal cyst is excised with the central part of the hyoid (Sistrunk procedure) to prevent recurrence; branchial cysts are excised after malignancy is excluded; pleomorphic adenoma is removed by superficial parotidectomy (it can become malignant and recurs if enucleated); submandibular stones are managed with hydration, sialogogues, massage, and stone or gland removal if recurrent.

**Stridor and airway emergencies:**
- Call for senior help (anaesthetics, ENT), keep the patient sitting upright, give oxygen, and avoid distressing them or instrumenting the throat.
- **Anaphylaxis**: **IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh** in adults, repeated every 5 minutes as needed, lie flat (or sit if breathing is difficult), IV fluids, and an adrenaline infusion if refractory, per the ASCIA guideline. Nebulised adrenaline can help upper airway oedema. Observe, and discharge with an adrenaline autoinjector, an ASCIA action plan and allergist referral.
- **ACE inhibitor angioedema**: bradykinin-mediated, so adrenaline, antihistamines and steroids work poorly. Stop the ACE inhibitor permanently, protect the airway early (awake fibreoptic intubation may be needed), and consider specific therapy (icatibant or C1 esterase inhibitor) with specialist advice. It can occur years after starting the drug.
- **Foreign body with complete obstruction**: basic life support choking algorithm (back blows, chest thrusts), then direct laryngoscopy and Magill forceps, or a surgical airway (cricothyroidotomy) as the last resort.
- **Tumour causing stridor**: senior airway management, often awake tracheostomy under local anaesthetic.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- Smoker with **hoarseness over 3 weeks**: the answer is **laryngoscopy (ENT referral)**, not antibiotics, PPIs or voice rest.
- **Earache with a normal ear** in a smoker who drinks: referred otalgia from a pharyngeal or laryngeal cancer.
- Hard neck node in an adult: **ultrasound-guided FNA** and ENT; **open excision biopsy is the wrong answer**.
- Midline lump moving with **tongue protrusion**: thyroglossal cyst. Moving only with swallowing: thyroid.
- Parotid lump with **facial weakness**: malignancy.
- Swollen lips and tongue with no urticaria on **perindopril or ramipril**: ACE inhibitor angioedema; stop the drug, protect the airway.
- Anaphylaxis: **IM adrenaline in the thigh first**, before antihistamines or steroids.

keyPoints: Red flags: hoarseness over 3 weeks, persistent neck lump, unilateral otalgia with a normal ear, dysphagia, non-healing mouth ulcer.
HPV-related oropharyngeal SCC is rising in younger non-smokers; lip SCC reflects Australian UV exposure.
Adult neck lump: examine, ultrasound-guided FNA, nasendoscopy; avoid open excision biopsy first.
Thyroglossal cyst moves with tongue protrusion; thyroid moves with swallowing.
Parotid lump with facial nerve palsy suggests malignancy; pleomorphic adenoma is the commonest salivary tumour.
Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (1:1000) into the thigh for adults, repeated every 5 minutes as needed.
ACE inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated and responds poorly to adrenaline; stop the drug and secure the airway.
redFlags: Hoarseness persisting beyond 3 weeks
Adult neck lump persisting beyond 3 weeks, especially hard or fixed
Unilateral otalgia with normal otoscopy
Progressive dysphagia, odynophagia or weight loss
Unilateral middle ear effusion in an adult
Stridor, drooling or tongue and lip swelling
Facial nerve weakness with a parotid lump

contrast.aspect: Typical head and neck cancer patient
contrast.india: Oral cavity SCC linked to chewing tobacco, betel quid and gutka, often advanced at presentation.
contrast.australia: Laryngeal and oral SCC in smokers and drinkers, rising HPV oropharyngeal SCC in younger adults, and UV-related lip SCC.

contrast.aspect: Tissue diagnosis of a neck node
contrast.india: Excision biopsy of a node is often done early, including for suspected TB.
contrast.australia: Ultrasound-guided FNA first and a search for a primary; open biopsy avoided until SCC is excluded.

flashcards.front: Duration of hoarseness that warrants laryngoscopy?
flashcards.back: **More than 3 weeks**, sooner in smokers or with other red flags.

flashcards.front: Midline neck lump that rises on tongue protrusion?
flashcards.back: **Thyroglossal duct cyst** (excised with the Sistrunk procedure).

flashcards.front: First-line tissue test for a persistent adult neck lump?
flashcards.back: **Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration**, not open excision biopsy.

flashcards.front: Adult anaphylaxis adrenaline dose?
flashcards.back: **0.5 mg IM** (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 minutes as needed.

flashcards.front: Mechanism of ACE inhibitor angioedema?
flashcards.back: **Bradykinin** accumulation; responds poorly to adrenaline, antihistamines and steroids.

quiz.stem:
A 63-year-old man presents to his GP in Townsville with a hoarse voice for 6 weeks. He has smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 40 years and drinks 4-5 beers a day. He has no fever, cough or sore throat. He was given a course of amoxicillin by another doctor 3 weeks ago with no improvement. Neck examination is normal.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: A trial of a proton pump inhibitor for 8 weeks
Voice rest and review in 1 month
quiz.explanation:
**Hoarseness persisting for more than 3 weeks**, especially in a **heavy smoker and drinker**, is a red flag for **laryngeal cancer** until proven otherwise. The vocal cords must be seen directly, so he needs **referral to ENT for flexible nasendoscopy/laryngoscopy**.

Reflux, voice overuse and viral laryngitis are common benign causes, but treating empirically in a high-risk patient delays the diagnosis. A chest X-ray is reasonable if a recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy from a lung apex tumour is suspected, but it does not replace laryngoscopy. The Optimal Care Pathway for head and neck cancers emphasises timely specialist referral.
whyWrong: An empirical PPI trial in a high-risk smoker delays diagnosis of cancer.
Voice rest is inappropriate once hoarseness has lasted over 3 weeks with risk factors.
A chest X-ray may be added but does not visualise the larynx.
Steroids could mask symptoms and do not establish a diagnosis.

quiz.stem:
A 52-year-old non-smoking man presents to his GP in Sydney with a painless lump in the left side of his neck that he noticed 5 weeks ago. It has not changed in size. Examination shows a 3 cm firm, mobile mass at the anterior border of the left sternocleidomastoid at the level of the hyoid. The left tonsil looks slightly larger than the right. He is otherwise well.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure him that it is a branchial cyst and review in 3 months
A course of cefalexin and review in 2 weeks
Refer for excision biopsy of the lump
Ultrasound of the neck with fine needle aspiration and ENT referral
Thyroid function tests and a thyroid uptake scan
quiz.explanation:
A persistent lateral neck lump in an adult over 40 is **malignant until proven otherwise**. A cystic or firm mass at the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid in a non-smoking middle-aged man, with **tonsillar asymmetry**, is classic for a nodal metastasis from **HPV-related oropharyngeal SCC**, which often masquerades as a branchial cyst.

The correct work-up is **ultrasound-guided FNA** plus **ENT referral for nasendoscopy** to find the primary, then cross-sectional imaging and p16/HPV testing. **Open excision biopsy is avoided** as a first step because it can seed tumour and compromise definitive neck treatment.
whyWrong: Diagnosing a branchial cyst in a 52-year-old without tissue risks missing a metastasis.
The lump has persisted 5 weeks without infective features; antibiotics delay diagnosis.
Open biopsy first can seed an SCC and compromise definitive treatment.
The mass is lateral and not thyroid in position; thyroid tests do not address it.
quiz.ausPearl: Australia's school-based HPV vaccination program covers boys and girls, partly to reduce future HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer.

quiz.stem:
A 66-year-old woman presents to an emergency department in Melbourne with 3 hours of progressive swelling of her lips and tongue. She has no itch, rash or wheeze. She takes perindopril for hypertension, which she has used for 4 years, and atorvastatin. She speaks in a thick voice but has no stridor. Heart rate is 88/min, blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, SpO2 97% on room air. She received IM adrenaline 0.5 mg on arrival with no improvement.

What is the most likely mechanism of her presentation?
quiz.explanation:
Angioedema of the lips and tongue **without urticaria, itch or wheeze** in a patient on an **ACE inhibitor** that fails to respond to adrenaline is **ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema**. ACE normally breaks down **bradykinin**; inhibiting it lets bradykinin accumulate, increasing vascular permeability. It can appear years after starting the drug.

Because it is not histamine-driven, adrenaline, antihistamines and corticosteroids work poorly. Management is to **stop the ACE inhibitor permanently**, monitor the airway closely with early senior anaesthetic and ENT involvement (intubation can become difficult quickly), and consider bradykinin-directed therapy such as icatibant or C1 esterase inhibitor with specialist advice. Angiotensin receptor blockers carry a small risk and should be used cautiously if at all afterwards.
whyWrong: IgE-mediated reactions cause urticaria and itch and usually respond to adrenaline.
Immune complex disease (type III) causes serum sickness or vasculitis, not isolated angioedema.
Statins are not a recognised cause of complement-mediated angioedema.
Atorvastatin does not cause direct histamine release.
